prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms trapped at the magic wavelength allow time and frequency to be measured at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep my round-1 position: a single-achievement prize for optical lattice clocks (B042) to Katori and Ye. Having read the full exchange, I think the case has become firmer, not weaker. The scientific core is a physical idea, the magic wavelength that cancels the light shift while thousands of atoms are interrogated without Doppler or recoil broadening, followed by an experimental road to about 1e-18 that has been reproduced by independent laboratories (JILA/NIST, RIKEN/Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB). That robustness across groups is the test I care most about, and B042 passes it more clearly than anything else on the shortlist. The new regime is already used for physics: gravitational redshift over millimetres, bounds on varying constants and on ultralight dark matter. It is also the one configuration that four members prefer outright and that all three B019 supporters name as their first fall-back, so it is the position on which the committee can most plausibly converge without anyone giving up a scientific conviction. I recommend a citation that is explicitly about the lattice clock, with Katori credited for the concept and first demonstration and Ye for taking it to record accuracy and stability, and with no reference to the comb or to the redefinition of the second, which is a metrological decision for others.
statement.case_against: The honest weaknesses are three. First, discovery versus instrument: Olsson and Mehlig weigh it nearer to a refinement of a metrology line already honoured in 2005 (combs) and 2012 (ion control). I think the many-atom, quantum-limited regime and the new measurements it opens are distinct, but this is a judgement and not a proof. Second, credit: Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Hinkley and Bloom were decisive in particular demonstrations, and Ye's cavity-stabilised-laser and comb work overlaps with the 2005 recognition, so the citation must be drawn tightly around the lattice clock to avoid re-crediting the comb. Third, timing: the redefinition of the second has not happened, and the largest scientific payoff of the clocks may still lie ahead. I do not think that is a reason to wait, since the prize rewards a demonstrated discovery and not a planned decision, but a member could reasonably disagree.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B019, says the single-particle band picture is quantitatively understood and that experiment has been reproduced by many groups, but concedes that the pairing mechanism is open and that if the committee finds the field too young, B042 is the better-settled discovery.
responses.response: I agree that the flat-band prediction and the observed correlated phases are well reproduced, and I agree that a narrow citation would be honest. Where we differ is the cost of waiting. Eight years after the experiments the pairing mechanism is still genuinely open and several correlated states are still disputed, and a few more years will probably clarify what the superconductivity is. Your own fall-back on B042 is what I rely on: if the committee cannot settle the Cao, Dean, Young and Lopes dos Santos credit questions in the citation wording, I can support B019 as my second choice with Jarillo-Herrero, MacDonald and Bistritzer, but I would not put it ahead of a candidate whose interpretation is already settled.

responses.point: Olsson asks what Ye's record-setting clocks add that is original and not only superior, and weighs lattice clocks nearer to an instrument, while naming B042 as the cleaner and more mature alternative to B019.
responses.response: This is the right question for Ye, and my answer is that the originality is in the regime and not only in the number. Moving from a few ions to thousands of neutral atoms, and reaching the point where the clock resolves the redshift across a millimetre-scale sample and probes systematic shifts at 1e-18, required new control of lattice shifts, collisions and laser coherence, and that changes what can be measured. I would still word Ye's part as realisation of the lattice clock at record accuracy and stability, not as a general contribution to precision spectroscopy. On your instrument concern, I note that your own criterion, a verified and reproducible discovery or invention, is met here by comparisons between independent national laboratories, which is a stronger reproduction record than most candidates on the list.

responses.point: Lindroth, in her case against B042, raises that Ye's cavity-stabilised-laser and comb work overlaps with the 2005 recognition and that Lemonde, Takamoto and the NIST and PTB groups have a real claim, and she questions B049 for its four names and its nearness to the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I accept her objection to B049 without reservation: the Blais and Girvin credit problem is real, and I should not press a second superconducting-circuit prize so soon after 2025, so I have dropped it from my configuration and I will not place it among my alternatives. On B042 I think her overlap point is best handled by the citation and not by changing the names. Because the comb enabled the clock but is not the clock, a text limited to the magic-wavelength lattice clock and its realisation at 1e-18 leaves 2005 where it was. For the Paris and PTB groups, I defer to her on atomic-physics priority, but I read their work as important confirmations and extensions that a two-name prize cannot capture, which is a pattern we accept on most instrument prizes.

responses.point: Danielsson now prefers B032 for Halzen and Spiering, arguing that the diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux is secure and a new messenger found in nature outweighs an instrument, while placing B042 third.
responses.response: I take his argument seriously, and I outside particle physics accept his reading that the diffuse flux is secure across channels. That is why I place B032 among my alternatives for the first time. What keeps it behind B042 for me is that individual source evidence is still at 3-4 sigma and that the Baikal, AMANDA and DUMAND pioneers are not covered by the proposed pair, so the pioneer credit is less clean than for the clock pair. I would also argue the discovery-versus-instrument question is not decisive between us, since B032 is also a detector-led observation. If the committee judges that a new window on nature must come before a measurement regime, I would not object to B032 as a second choice.

responses.point: Mehlig, moving from KPZ to B019, argues that the moire mechanism is simple and analysable and that six of eight members ranked it, while accepting that maturity and attribution are the main reservations and that B042 has the cleaner two-person attribution.
responses.response: I agree with his two reservations and that they are the ones that matter, and I accept his point that Bistritzer-MacDonald plus Jarillo-Herrero is a very attractive prediction-and-experiment pairing. I would simply weigh the unsettled mechanism more heavily than he does. A prediction followed by a discovery is a strong template, but the Nobel citation must rest on what is understood, and the clocks offer that now while graphene is better with a few more years of data. His own concession that B042 is the cleaner attribution is, in my view, the practical reason to take B042 first and B019 afterwards.

uncertainties: Whether Lemonde, Ludlow or another early contributor has a stronger claim than Ye on the first lattice-clock demonstrations. I cannot settle this from the nominations and the experts should confirm.

Whether a citation can be worded to credit Ye for realisation at record accuracy without appearing to re-credit the 2005 comb work, and whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as a discovery or invention under the will.
Whether the redefinition of the second, expected in the next decade, would make a later award more or less defensible. I now lean to not waiting, but I am not certain.
Whether B019 could prove the more consequential choice in ten years if the pairing mechanism is clarified, and whether I am underweighting the field because it lies outside my own.
statement.conflict_note: My disclosure is updated. I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work on superconducting circuits at Chalmers, so B049 (circuit QED), B051 (optomechanics with superconducting qubits) and B038 (quantum computing foundations) are in my own field or national programme, and I would recuse myself on those ballots. I no longer support any of them in my configuration or alternatives. Chalmers also hosted 2025 laureates Martinis and Clarke as guests. I have no connection to Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer, Halzen or Spiering that I know of, and I do not believe any recusal is needed for B042, B019 or B032.
